metadata.title: Why Two Well-Behaved Agents Make One Badly-Behaved System
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why two well-behaved agents make one badly-behaved system? Lands the carry-out that downstream agents condition on upstream outputs as ground truth, so errors compound rather than add.
metadata.one_flag: B10 — deterministic typed schemas vs generative context passing

beats.narration_text: Agent A errs two percent of the time. Agent B errs three percent. Naturally, we expect their combined pipeline to fail about five percent of the time. But in practice, it can fail on a third of its runs. Let's see why.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on '5% of the time?', corrects to 'a third of its runs?'

props.text:
Agent A errs 2% of the time.
Agent B errs 3% of the time.
Why does their pipeline fail 5% of the time?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Writer types naive framing, hesitates, corrects to a third of its runs. Liam reads over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: Suppose you build an autonomous pipeline. You test Agent A alone on ten thousand records: ninety-eight percent accuracy. You test Agent B alone: ninety-seven percent accuracy. Both benchmarks look pristine.

shot.new_visual_element: Isolated benchmark test cards for Agent A (98%) and Agent B (97%)

production_viz.label: Isolated Agent Benchmarks
production_viz.mechanic: Two test cards side by side showing Agent A (98% pass) and Agent B (97% pass) on clean validation datasets.

beats.narration_text: You chain them together in production. Agent A extracts data from raw files, and Agent B formulates actions from those summaries. But when you monitor the live system, nearly thirty percent of customer tasks fail.

shot.new_visual_element: Chained pipeline in production showing 30% system failure rate

production_viz.label: Chained Pipeline Failure
production_viz.mechanic: Pipeline diagram connecting Agent A to Agent B resulting in a 30% failure rate badge highlighted in terracotta.

beats.narration_text: To understand this collapse, look at the pipeline as a relay chain. Agent A passes an intermediate document to Agent B, which passes an execution plan to the world. The entire system hinges on what happens during that handoff.

shot.new_visual_element: The relay chain anchor: Agent A passing document payload to Agent B to Output

production_viz.label: The Relay Chain Anchor
production_viz.mechanic: A 3-node relay pipeline with document payload being transferred across the interface boundary.

beats.narration_text: Intuition tells us errors should simply add. If Agent A has a two percent chance of slipping, and Agent B has a three percent chance, independent probability says about ninety-five percent of runs should succeed.

shot.new_visual_element: Naive independent error probability formula and 95% success bar

production_viz.label: The Addition Fallacy
production_viz.mechanic: Independent probability formula P(fail) ≈ 2% + 3% = 5% with green 95% success bar.

beats.narration_text: That arithmetic assumes agents are independent coin flips on clean, isolated inputs. But Agent B is not acting on clean input. Agent B receives Agent A's output as its unverified reality.

shot.new_visual_element: Falsifying the independent assumption: Agent B input is contaminated upstream output

production_viz.label: Falsifying Independence
production_viz.mechanic: The independent coin-flip model struck down in terracotta; input arrow highlighted as unverified upstream state.

beats.narration_text: Watch what happens inside the handoff document. On two percent of runs, Agent A makes a minor, plausible error—say, shifting a delivery date or dropping a constraint. To Agent A, it is one misplaced token.

shot.new_visual_element: Manim accumulate move: Agent A outputs document with 1 subtle error block

production_viz.label: Upstream Error Seed
production_viz.mechanic: Document payload rendered with lines of text; a single token slips to red terracotta.

beats.narration_text: Now Agent B takes over. Agent B has no memory of the original source text and no reason to doubt the document. It conditions on Agent A's error as absolute ground truth, actively reasoning around the false premise.

shot.new_visual_element: Manim accumulate move: Agent B ingests document and spawns 3 dependent errors

production_viz.label: Downstream Conditioning
production_viz.mechanic: Agent B consumes the document; three dependent inference branches spawn in terracotta from the single faulty premise.

beats.narration_text: The error multiplies. From that single false date, Agent B generates conflicting schedule bookings, cancels valid orders, and issues false emergency alerts. One minor upstream slip accumulates into complete downstream chaos.

shot.new_visual_element: Manim accumulate move: 7 cascading error blocks flood the execution payload

production_viz.label: Error Accumulation
production_viz.mechanic: The execution plan explodes with 7 red terracotta error blocks; compound failure dominates.

beats.narration_text: This is why per-agent benchmarks are blind. In isolation, each agent was tested on pristine, valid data. In the relay chain, Agent B operates in an out-of-distribution state created by Agent A. Per-agent validation cannot see the interaction term.

shot.new_visual_element: The Anchor Payoff: Isolated Benchmark (98%/97%) vs Relay System (30% Failure)

production_viz.label: The Interaction Term
production_viz.mechanic: Comparison diagram showing clean test distribution vs out-of-distribution relay handoff highlighting the unseen interaction term.

beats.narration_text: One flag—how rapidly errors compound depends on the interface. In rigid pipelines with typed schemas, an invalid upstream value throws an immediate exception. But in generative agent workflows, downstream models hallucinate plausible justifications for bad premises, supercharging the cascade.

shot.new_visual_element: Typed schema interface (fails fast) vs Generative context interface (cascade accelerates)

production_viz.label: The Interface Flag
production_viz.mechanic: Two contrasting paths: typed schema halts immediately vs generative context weaves plausible confabulation.

beats.narration_text: So validating individual agents to ninety-nine percent accuracy guarantees almost nothing about the safety of their pipeline, if intermediate handoffs pass unchecked natural language.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction A: 99% isolated accuracy struck through in terracotta

production_viz.label: Direction A: Isolation Blindness
production_viz.mechanic: Isolated high score card struck through: unchecked handoffs lead to systemic collapse.

beats.narration_text: And yet the fix is not to abandon agent chains. It is to place explicit boundary invariants between them—validating handoff contracts against ground truth rather than trusting the upstream agent's word.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction B: Boundary invariants verifying contracts between agents

production_viz.label: Direction B: Boundary Invariants
production_viz.mechanic: Verification barrier between Agent A and Agent B checking invariants against world state.

beats.narration_text: Downstream agents treat upstream outputs as ground truth, so errors do not add—they compound.

props.quote: Downstream agents treat upstream outputs as ground truth, so errors do not add—they compound.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take a multi-agent workflow in your stack where Agent B acts on Agent A's output. Inject a subtle, plausible error into Agent A's handoff document—a shifted date, a flipped polarity, or an omitted constraint. Run Agent B on that corrupted input. Does Agent B flag the anomaly, or does it elaborate on the false premise? Audit how your pipeline handles upstream errors before chaining your next agent. Liam, in for Bear.
